newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE 100 ends at a new record, lifted by Dow.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE 100 ends at a new record, lifted by Dow.

text.p: Leading UK shares scaled new peaks on Friday, inspired by bullish Wall Street and shrugging off uncertainties created by the Labour Party's historic sweep to power.
The benchmark index rose early on, defying initial expectations for big drop, and then gathered pace in the final hours of the session as Wall Street leapt.

The blue chip index added 10.6 points to close at 4,455.6, as advancers led decliners by a margin of about five to three. But trading was relatively light, with SEAQ volume registering only 569.5 million shares at 1539 GMT.
The election result, said one senior London trader, was "almost an anticlimax."

"But the market's reaction was perfectly reasonable. Labour's win was rock solid and to some degree, an election of uncertainty has been removed," he added. "The fundamentals are good and the market has liquidity"

UK shares drew the strength to climb into record territory from Wall Street, where the Dow cleared the 7,000 mark after U.S. employment data showed a decline in wages and a smaller-than-expected 142,000 non-farm jobs were created in April.
The Dow was up about 24 points when London markets closed.
Yet economists said a dip in the U.S. unemployment rate leaves open the door for the Federal Reserve to tighten credit further.
Yet the immediate focus for the British share market is next week's UK monetary meeting on Wednesday, when the newly-appointed chancellor Gordon Brown will meet with Bank of England Eddie George.
UK financial markets have been bracing themselves for weeks, if not months, for an interest rate hike in the wake of the election.

"There are a lot of hurdles in front of the market at the moment," said Cory Miller, UK equity strategist with Credit Lyonnais Laing. "I think Labour will want to get the bad news out of the way early on ... Eddie George has been pushing for a rate rise for a while now."
Short sterling interest rate futures were reflecting expectations for a 50 basis point interest rate hike, yet many strategists were predicting a rise only 25 basis points.

"No rate rise or (a rise of) 50 basis points might cause the market to reassess," said Peter Warburton, an economist with Robert Fleming Securities. "We'll have to see how much they tighten. A quarter of a point would be just a symbolic move."
"I don't think anyone is expecting no change in rates. The only point of disagreement is the amount by which they'll be raised," another London dealer added.
Losses in the utility sector, vulnerable to "windfall" and other new taxes under the incoming Labour government, were offset by a strong rebound in shares in major UK exporters as sterling weakened.
United Utilities dropped 22p to 647, National Power fell 17-1/2p at 515 and PowerGen lost 23p to 630-1/2.

Exporting stocks, the victims of sterling's strength, rose as the currency wobbled on the foreign exchange markets. British Steel advanced 7-1/4p to 146-1/2, while Siebe Plc rose 19p to 936-1/2. TI Group jumped 10p to 543-1/2p.
